newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST. WEEK AHEAD - Blue-chip blues, rate fears.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST. WEEK AHEAD - Blue-chip blues, rate fears.

text.p: The stock market's rollercoaster ride is likely to continue this week as uncertainty over the dollar, interest rates and blue chip issues provide potential hairpin turns.
"For the week I'd expect wide swings with not much of a gain or loss," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst for Tucker Anthony.
The Federal Reserve Open Market committee meets Tuesday to determine the fate of interest rates in August.
Technology benchmarks Dell and Hewlett-Packard will report their earnings amid fears that the strong corporate profits that have driven the market's record-breaking run will slow.

"My guess is that we're going to see some more bloodletting in the large cap types," said Bill Meehan, national sales desk manager for Prudential Securities. "We're likely to get a bit more of funk but some value investors could step up to the plate."

The Dow Jones industrial average on Friday capped one of the volatile weeks in recent history, slumping 247.37 points, or 3.1 percent, at 7,694.66, which was the second-biggest point loss ever. The drop was the steepest point fall since Oct. 19, 1987, the so-called Black Monday when the Dow sank 508 points, or 23 percent, to 1,738.74.

The selloff contributed to a loss for the week of 336.56 points, making it the largest weekly loss in the history of the average amid fears that blue chips, bonds and the greenback were all losing their luster.
Phil Orlando of Value Line Asset Management said that he did not expect the Fed to raise interest rates Tuesday's meeting.
"Our anticipation is that we'll get no activity from the Fed. We're probably on hold for the Sept. 30 meeting as well given the tone of the inflation data."
Prudential's Meehan said he expected "A little more pressure on Coke, Gillette and Procter & Gamble."

Investors have been concerned since Coca-Cola warned earlier this month that its earnings would slow in the third quarter of the year. Gillette tumbled Friday on news that it had guided analysts' earnings estimates lower.
"Unless we see a decent rally in the bond market we'll see some uncertainty," Meehan said.
"We'll have a bit more of the same, the market has given back some momentum," said Alan Ackerman, an analyst for Fahnestock & Co.
"Despite (Friday's) action I would expect the bond market to firm up early next week," said Tucker Anthony's Laubscher. "But we think you'll have a bear market in the next six months to a year."
